title: Your weekly rest
hookLine: design your digital sabbath: when, how long, what instead

lines: SHABBAT, THE DRAWER, BOREDOM, THE MEAL.
cards: Right before rest, a voice tends to speak up: you haven't done enough to deserve a break yet. It gets in almost everybody's way, and it's worth naming.
This week brought Shabbat, the original weekly rest; one hour with the phone in a drawer; the boredom that comes first, and the noticing after; one meal with the people instead of the feed.
Today turns the experiment into a habit: you design your own weekly rest.

teach.b: Notice something about the Sabbath from the start of this week. It doesn't wait for you to finish. It arrives at sunset on Friday whether the work is done or not.

teach.h: AS IF ALL YOUR WORK IS DONE.
teach.b: The medieval commentator Rashi, reading the command to work six days and do all your work, explains it this way: when the Sabbath comes, it should feel as if all your work is done. Not because it is.
Because you're allowed to stop anyway. The Gospels have their own saying about it, in a different setting: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath."
Each tradition keeps rest in its own way and for its own reasons. But both push against the same modern habit: treating rest as a prize for productivity. Rest isn't earned.
It's part of the week. So, the design, in three questions.
When? A regular slot, like Saturday morning, Sunday after lunch, or every weeknight after eight. Regular matters more than long.
How long? Start with what you'll actually keep. Three hours you keep beats a whole day you abandon, and you can grow it.
And the one people forget: what instead?
An empty rest fills right back up with scrolling. So choose what goes in the space: a walk, a long meal, a book, a nap, friends, prayer if you pray.
A rest with a time, a length and a plan, written down, is much harder to skip than a vague good intention.

how: People who keep a digital sabbath usually set a regular weekly window, often an evening or a weekend day, put devices away, and plan what they'll do instead, like walks, meals, reading or rest.

games.q: it's time for your weekly rest, and your to-do list isn't finished. what does today's teaching say?
o: finish the list first; then you've earned it.
rest anyway, as if the work were done.
skip rest this week and double it next week.
games.why: rest anyway. as Rashi reads it, when the Sabbath comes it should feel as if all your work is done. rest isn't earned.

practice: Let a day and a time appear, then a length you'd actually keep, then two things that will fill the space, and say each one inside. Picture the rest beginning: phone into the drawer, a lamp on, a deep breath.
If the voice says you haven't earned it, let it talk, and rest anyway.
